el.e: From Middle English, from Old English el, from Latin el (the name of the letter L).
el.g: The name of the Latin script letter L/l.
The cardinal number occurring after dek and before do in a duodecimal system. Written ↋, decimal value 11.

elder.e: From Middle English eldre, from Old English eldra, yldra, ieldra, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô. The vowel change from a to e triggered by the following i is called umlaut or I-mutation.
elder.g: A leader or senior member of a tribe or community, often of considerable age, respected as an authority figure, especially in a counselling,

elect.e: Borrowed from Latin ēlēctus, past participle of ēligō (“to pick out, choose, elect”), from ē- (“out”) + legō (“to pick out, pick, gather, collect, etc.”); see legend.

election.e: From Middle English eleccioun, eleccion, from Anglo-Norman eleccioun, from Latin ēlectiōn-, stem of ēlectiō (“choice, selection”), from ēligō (“to pluck out, to choose”). Equivalent to elect + -ion.
election.g: A process of choosing a leader, members of parliament, councillors, or other representatives by popular vote.

elegant.e: From Late Middle English elegaunt, from Middle French elegant, ultimately from Latin ēlegāns, collateral form of present participle of ēligere, from ex- (“out of, from”) + legō (“choose, select, appoint”).
elegant.g: Characterised by or exhibiting elegance; having grace, refinement, or tasteful simplicity.

element.e: From Middle English element, from Old French element, from Latin elementum (“a first principle, element, rudiment”) (see further etymology there).
element.g: One of the simplest or essential parts or principles of which anything consists, or upon which the constitution or fundamental powers of any

elementary.e: From Middle English elementare, from Latin elementārius (“elementary”), from elementum (“one of the four elements of antiquity; fundamentals”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, element + -ary.
elementary.g: Relating to the basic, essential or fundamental part of something.

elevate.e: From Middle English elevaten (“to raise up, erect; to elate, inflate (e.g. with pride); (alchemy) to vaporize; (of a bone, excressence, blood vessel) to protrude”).
elevate.g: To raise (something) to a higher position.

elevate.e: From Middle English elevat(e) (“(in physical elevation, in rank, in altitude above the horizon) high”, also used as the past participle of elevaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

eleven.e: From Middle English elleven, enleven, eleven, from Old English endleofan; from Proto-Germanic *ainalif (“one left”) (i.e., one left over after having already counted to ten), a compound of *ainaz and *-lif, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, remain”).
eleven.g: The cardinal number occurring after ten and before twelve. Represented as 11 in Arabic digits.

eleventh.e: From Middle English elleventhe, from elleven + -the, equivalent to eleven + -th. This re-formation replaced inherited forms such as ellefte, enlefte, from Old English endlefta, from Proto-Germanic *ainaliftô.
eleventh.g: The ordinal form of the number eleven.

elicit.e: Borrowed from Latin elicitus from eliciō (“draw forth”).
elicit.g: To evoke, educe (emotions, feelings, responses, etc.); to generate, obtain, or provoke as a response or answer.

eliminate.e: Borrowed from Latin ēlīminātus, perfect passive participle of ēlīminō (“to turn out of doors, banish”), from ē- + līmen (“a threshold”, līmin- in compounds) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), akin to Latin līmes (“a boundary”); see also English limit and limen.
eliminate.g: To completely remove, get rid of, put an end to.

elite.e: From Middle English elit, from Old French elit, eslit (“chosen, elected”) past participle of elire, eslire (“to choose, elect”), from Latin eligere (“to choose, elect”), with past participle electus; see elect.
elite.g: Of high birth or social position; aristocratic or patrician.

elm.e: From Middle English elme, elm, from Old English elm, from Proto-West Germanic *elm, from Proto-Germanic *elmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).
elm.g: A tree of the genus Ulmus of the family Ulmaceae, large deciduous trees with alternate stipulate leaves and small apetalous flowers.

eloquence.e: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia.
eloquence.g: The quality of artistry and persuasiveness in speech or writing.

eloquent.e: From Old French eloquent, from Latin eloquens (“speaking, having the faculty of speech, eloquent”), present participle of eloquor (“to speak out”), from e (“out”) + loquor (“to speak”).

else.e: From Middle English ells, elles, from Old English elles (“other, otherwise, different”), from Proto-West Germanic *alljas, from Proto-Germanic *aljas (“of another, of something else”), genitive of *aljaz (“other”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos, from *h₂el- (“other”).
else.g: Other; in addition to previously mentioned items.

elsewhere.e: From Middle English elswher, from Old English elles hwǣr and elles hwerġen (“elsewhere”); corresponding with else + where.
elsewhere.g: Synonym of somewhere else: in, at, or to some other place.

elude.e: From Latin ēlūdō (“to evade, elude”), from ē- (“out of”, short form of ex-) + lūdō (“to play; to trick”).
elude.g: To evade or escape from (someone or something), especially by using cunning or skill.

old.e: From Middle English old, oold, from Old English ald, eald (“old, aged, ancient, antique, primeval”), from Proto-West Germanic *ald, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz (“grown-up”), originally a participle form, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós (“grown, tall, big”).
old.g: Of an object, concept, relationship, etc., having existed for a relatively long period of time.
